summary: Defines Bundle Protocol Security, which provides data integrity and confidentiality for the Bundle Protocol used in delay-tolerant networking. It lets parts of a bundle be protected as they pass through a network. Specific algorithms are left to separate security contexts.

plainLanguage.summary:
BPSec adds two kinds of extra block to a bundle in a delay-tolerant network. One signs a block so that tampering can be detected; the other encrypts it so that the nodes carrying it cannot read it.

Every node along the path can add its own protection, and each node handles only the parts addressed to it. The algorithms and keys come from a named security context, so different networks can use different ones.

how to secure delay tolerant networking
what is a security context in bpsec
subtitle: Integrity and confidentiality for bundles in delay-tolerant networks, applied block by block with pluggable security contexts.

tldr.problem: The Bundle Protocol runs in stressed networks with long delays and intermittent links, where data waits at rest in nodes and there may be no live contact with a certificate authority. Usual transport security does not fit.
tldr.mechanism: BPSec adds two extension blocks to a bundle: a Block Integrity Block (BIB) that protects the plaintext of target blocks, and a Block Confidentiality Block (BCB) that encrypts them. The algorithms and keys come from a separate, named security context.
tldr.outcome: Different blocks can get different protection from different nodes, and any node can verify or process the blocks it is responsible for. Key management and security policy are left to each network.

today: RFC 9172 was published in January 2022 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The default security contexts it refers to are defined separately in RFC 9173.

sections.title: Why Bundles Need Their Own Security
sections.content:
This document defines security features for the Bundle Protocol (BP) of RFC 9171, for use in Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN). The Bundle Protocol sits at the application layer of a set of constituent networks and forms a store-carry-forward overlay: a node that receives a bundle holds on to it and carries it until it can forward it.

The environment is deliberately hostile: intermittent connectivity, large and variable delays, asymmetric data rates and high bit error rates. The protocol should be assumed to run in an untrusted network, and the usual transport security mechanisms do not cover the conditions. Data may sit at rest in a node for a long time, storage space is a critical resource that an unauthorised user might want to consume, and there may be no regular contact with a central authority such as a certificate authority.

BPSec provides two services. Integrity services make it possible to detect changes to a target block, whether caused by a processing error, the environment or an attacker. Confidentiality services make the target data unreadable to nodes that do not hold special information; confidentiality covers the contents of the target, not the fact that confidentiality exists.

Hop-by-hop authentication is explicitly not a supported service. The RFC gives two reasons: in an overlay, nodes that are adjacent in the overlay need not be adjacent physically, so hop-by-hop authentication is hard or impossible to enforce; and it cannot be deployed where neighbouring nodes have incompatible security capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle is carried across a network that may lose contact for days. It sits in storage at intermediate nodes, and those nodes may be hostile. Ordinary transport security does not fit that, so BPSec protects individual parts of the bundle as it travels.

sections.title: The Design Decisions
sections.content:
Five decisions shape the protocol.

  • Block-level granularity. Different blocks in a bundle hold different kinds of information and need different protection. A payload block might be encrypted while an extension block carrying a summary of the payload is signed but left readable, so that waypoints can use it.
  • Multiple security sources. A bundle can carry several security blocks from different nodes. A source may sign the payload, and a later waypoint may encrypt it. Implementations MUST NOT assume that every block has the same protection.
  • Mixed security policy. Nodes may differ in what they do. A waypoint might verify an integrity service even though it is not the destination, might terminate the service and remove the block, or might refuse to process security blocks at all unless it is the destination.
  • User-defined security contexts. A security context is the set of assumptions, algorithms, configuration and policy used to implement a security service. BPSec provides a mechanism to define them, and users may pick a registered context and adjust its parameters. One network might prefer SHA2 and another SHA3.
  • Deterministic processing. When a node must process more than one security block, the order is fixed and identical everywhere. The RFC accepts a loss of flexibility in exchange for determinism.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of a bundle can be protected differently and by a different node. The order in which a node handles the protection blocks is fixed, so that every node in the network does the same thing in the same sequence.

sections.title: The Two Security Blocks
sections.content:
The protocol defines two block types. The Block Integrity Block (BIB) protects the integrity of its target blocks in plaintext. Any node on the path from the BIB's security source to the bundle destination may verify it, and waypoints add or remove BIBs according to their policy. The Block Confidentiality Block (BCB) says that its targets were encrypted at the BCB's security source, and it also carries integrity protection for the ciphertext it produced.

Both block types share the same internal layout, which the RFC calls the Abstract Security Block. Its fields appear in a fixed order: security targets, security context identifier, security context flags, security source, optional security context parameters, and security results. Security targets are the block numbers of the blocks being protected, as a CBOR array of unsigned integers with at least one entry and no duplicates. The context identifier names the security context to use. The flags say which optional fields are present; bit 0 means that security context parameters are present. The security source names the node that inserted the block. The parameters are a list of identifier and value pairs. The results are a list, one entry per target, each holding identifier and value pairs such as a signature or an authentication tag.

Each security service may be applied to a target only once in a bundle, so two security blocks of the same type cannot share a target. One block may cover several targets when they all use the same service, the same context parameters and the same security source.
sections.plainLanguage: Both kinds of block carry the same list of fields: which blocks they protect, which security context to use, who added them, any settings for that context, and the results of running it. A block can protect several blocks at once, as long as they are treated the same way.

sections.title: Rules for Combining Integrity and Confidentiality Blocks
sections.content:
The two block types are meant to be independent, but a conflict arises when they share a target. If a BCB encrypts a block that a BIB also covers, a waypoint cannot check the BIB, because the shared target is now ciphertext. The RFC sets out rules to avoid that.

When a BCB is added and its targets match all the targets of an existing BIB, the existing BIB must also be encrypted, either by adding a new BCB that targets it or by adding it to the BCB's target list. When a BCB's targets match only some of a BIB's targets, the matching results must be moved out of that BIB into a new BIB, and the new BIB must then be encrypted. A BIB must not be added for a target that a BCB already protects, and a BIB's integrity value must not be checked when the BIB itself or its target is protected by a BCB.

These rules impose an ordering: for any given target, BIBs must be added before BCBs, and that order must be kept whether the node is creating the whole bundle or adding to one that already has security blocks. When a node wants both a plaintext integrity signature and encryption for the same target, it must use a single BCB whose security context produces the integrity result as one of its security results, rather than adding a BIB and then a BCB.
sections.plainLanguage: If a block is both signed and encrypted, the signature has to be encrypted too, or nobody can check it. The rule is simple: sign first, then encrypt, and never sign a block that is already encrypted.

sections.title: Canonical Forms and Security Processing
sections.content:
Before a cipher suite sees a target, the target is put into a canonical form, so that the same bytes are hashed or encrypted whether they were encoded one way on the wire and another way in memory. For blocks other than the primary block, only the block-type-specific data field is encrypted, and the other fields are left alone, though they may be treated as associated authenticated data. CBOR values are canonicalized using the rules for deterministically encoded CBOR from RFC 8949, and reserved flags are set to zero in a canonical form because they may change in transit.

When a bundle arrives, security blocks are processed in a fixed order: where a BIB and a BCB share a target, the BCB is evaluated first and the BIB second. For a BCB, the receiving node checks whether it is the security acceptor for any of the operations. If it is, it processes those operations and removes the operation-specific information before delivering data or forwarding the bundle, and the BCB is removed once all its operations are gone. If the node is the bundle destination, it must decrypt any remaining BCBs. If an encrypted payload cannot be decrypted, the bundle must be discarded; if some other encrypted target cannot be decrypted, that target and the blocks associated with it are discarded.

For a BIB, a node that is not the security acceptor may still verify the signature to avoid forwarding corrupt data, and if the check fails it must handle the target according to local policy. If the check passes it must not remove the security operation before forwarding. When a bundle payload is fragmented, security blocks are never applied to the fragment itself, and confidentiality should be applied before any fragmentation happens.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node puts the data into a standard form before checking or encrypting it, so the result does not depend on how the bytes happened to be encoded. On receipt, encrypted blocks are handled first and signed blocks second, because a signed block cannot be checked until the data it covers has been decrypted.

sections.title: Security Reason Codes and Policy
sections.content:
The Bundle Protocol lets a node report what it did with a bundle to the bundle's report-to address, and the report can carry a reason code explaining why. BPSec defines five security reason codes, numbered 12 to 16 for Bundle Protocol version 7: Missing security operation, when a bundle lacked a required operation; Unknown security operation, when the node cannot understand the operation, for example because it refers to an unknown security context; Unexpected security operation, when the node is neither verifier nor acceptor for at least one operation, which is not an error; Failed security operation, when an operation did not process as expected; and Conflicting security operation, when two operations in the bundle are not conformant and processing could not continue.

The RFC warns that sending these reports can itself weaken the network if an unintended recipient intercepts them. Policy should say when they may be sent. The examples given are: when the report-to address is verified as unchanged from the bundle source, for instance by putting a BIB on the primary block; when the report itself is encrypted by a BCB; when the report only concerns non-operational data or test data; and when it only concerns non-operational security contexts or test keys.

Key management is not part of this specification. BPSec assumes keys are handled as a separate part of network management, and neither defines nor requires a particular strategy.
sections.plainLanguage: A node can send a report saying why it dropped or passed on a bundle, with a code for the security reason. Those reports can leak information, so a policy should say when they are allowed. How keys are shared and managed is left entirely to the network operator.

sections.title: Threats and Security Contexts
sections.content:
The threat model assumes the delay-tolerant network, or much of it, is under the control of an attacker who can receive, examine, modify, forward and generate bundles. Three kinds of attacker node are distinguished by the key material they hold. An unprivileged node has only publicly shared material. A legitimate node also holds material provisioned for it. A privileged node holds material provisioned for it and for the endpoints, which amounts to a compromise of the network; BPSec has no mechanism to detect or remove such a node. If one shared key set is used for every node, then a legitimate node is equivalent to a privileged one, which is why the RFC does not recommend that arrangement.

Against eavesdropping, the protection is the BCB, which encrypts its target. The RFC notes that bundles may persist in a DTN for days or even years, so a long-lived bundle gives an attacker many chances to try to recover the key or the plaintext offline. Against modification, the BIB detects changes to the plaintext it protects. Against topology attacks, in which an attacker removes or reorders bundles, the bundle protocol itself is the defence, since BPSec does not address the security of the DTN underneath. Against message injection, the integrity service detects bundles that were fabricated or altered.

The security context registry has a registration policy of Specification Required, and its value range is a signed 16-bit integer. Negative identifiers are reserved for local or site-specific use, and zero is for non-operational testing only. The RFC requires that security contexts be mandatory to implement for interoperability, and gives rules for how they are identified and configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The design assumes the network may be under the control of an attacker who can read and alter bundles. Signing detects altered bundles and encryption hides their contents. A node that holds the keys of the endpoints is treated as a compromise, and the protocol has no way to detect or remove it.

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR PROCESSING A RECEIVED BUNDLE

items.title: BCBs before BIBs
items.text: Where a BIB and a BCB share a target, the BCB is evaluated first.

items.title: The acceptor acts
items.text: A node that is the security acceptor processes the operations and removes them from the block.

items.title: The destination decrypts
items.text: A node that is the bundle destination must decrypt any BCB still in the bundle.

items.title: Verification is optional
items.text: A node that is not the acceptor may still check a signature, but must keep the operation if the check passes.

items.desc: The bundle lacked a required operation.

items.label: Unknown security operation
items.desc: The node cannot understand the operation or its context.

items.label: Unexpected security operation
items.desc: The node is neither verifier nor acceptor for it; not an error.

items.label: Failed security operation
items.desc: The operation did not process as expected.

items.label: Conflicting security operation
items.desc: The bundle breaks the specification and processing could not continue.
